endorsements.title: Health Equity Across the AI Lifecycle (HEAAL) framework
endorsements.issuer: Health AI Partnership; PLOS Digital Health (PMID 38723025, doi:10.1371/journal.pdig.0000390)
endorsements.quote: Prospective implementation of the AI solution with proactive outreach to conduct appropriate workup and diagnosis for all high- risk patients will be required to assess the impact on health equity.

evidence.title: Automated Calls Added to SMS Reminders Reduce Missed Appointments among High-Risk Patients
evidence.venue: NEJM catalyst innovations in care delivery
evidence.outcome: Appointment completion by race after pairing risk flags with supportive outreach
evidence.effect: Supportive IVR outreach to high-risk patients increased completion most among Black patients, reducing a preexisting equity gap.
evidence.quote: It also increased appointment completion rates the most among Black patients, helping to reduce a preexisting equity gap.

commentary.bottom_line: One large randomized trial in a real deployment found that supportive automated phone outreach to patients flagged as high risk raised appointment completion, with the largest gain among Black patients and a smaller preexisting gap by race. No study compared supportive outreach directly with punitive responses such as overbooking or exclusion, and none measured punitive harms.

perspectives.view: A single randomized trial of 59,994 patients supports the practice. Certainty begins high for randomized designs and is lowered here for indirectness. The trial tested one outreach mode, interactive voice response, on one outcome, appointment completion. The summary does not show that the comparison arm involved punitive actions. With no replication in other settings, the certainty is rated low.

The trial reported results by race and found that completion rose most among Black patients, which narrowed an existing gap. This suggests that supportive use of a risk flag may reduce rather than widen disparities on this outcome. The summary gives no results by insurance type, language, or literacy.

The trial measured whether patients completed appointments. It did not count denied or overbooked visits, dismissals, or other exclusionary events. It therefore shows a benefit of outreach but does not show that pairing flags with outreach prevents punitive use of the same flags elsewhere in the organization.

The outreach in the trial was automated interactive voice response delivered in a real deployment at large scale. This suggests that a supportive response can run in routine workflows without adding staff contact for every flagged patient. The trial did not test the medical workup or social support outreach that the HEAAL framework describes.

In the trial, a high-risk flag led to a reminder and support rather than a penalty, and more patients kept their visits. The outreach was automated, however, and the summary does not report whether patients could reach a person or how they viewed the calls.

commentary.research_gap: Trials are needed that compare supportive outreach with punitive responses such as overbooking or discharge from a practice. These trials should measure exclusionary events, access, and clinical outcomes, and they should test human-delivered medical and social support alongside automated calls.
commentary.underserved_note: The one trial reported effects by race but did not report results for Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy patients. Automated voice outreach may perform differently for patients with limited English or low literacy, so the benefit for these groups remains untested.
